The mobile app's palette: navy ink on warm paper, white forms that float on a soft warm shadow, lavender rows inside them, and RoVR blue kept for action. Red appears only when something is wrong.
DM Sans throughout, as on the landing page. Headlines are medium weight and set tight; everything else is regular, medium or semibold at its natural spacing.
Forms are generously curved and controls are full pills: 14px fields, 20px inner cards, 28px forms, 36px for the hero. Compact density tightens the same components for the provider app.

Controls respond like physical things: they sink under the pointer and spring back, and one highlight glides between items. Overlays do the opposite. They arrive quickly and plainly, because a dialog should not perform.
RoVR uses the Lucide icon set through lucide-react: outlined icons at a 1.5 stroke, 16px inside controls. One set for both apps.
A stack of headings that each open a panel. Use it for questions and answers and for long records where people need one or two sections at a time.
ConfirmDialog is a blocking question before an action that cannot be undone. Use it for deleting, signing and removing; use a toast with Undo when the action can be reversed.
A person's photo, or their initials when there is no photo. Use it wherever a patient or clinician is named.
Five tones in three forms: a tag, a status dot with text, and a count. It replaces the two dozen one-off status badges in the apps today.
A page-wide message above the content: scheduled downtime, an expired session, read-only mode. Use a callout for a message about one part of the page.
Replaces content in place by blurring the old out as the new sharpens in, as the mobile app does. Use it for icon swaps, labels that change in place and counters.
Shows where a page sits in the app and links back up each level. Use it on pages two or more levels deep, such as a result inside a patient's chart.
One Button with seven variants and three sizes. It replaces the six or seven button components in each app today.
A month grid for choosing one day or a range, shown directly on the page. It is what DatePicker opens, and it pairs with TimeSlots in the booking flow.
An inline message that stays on the page, next to the thing it is about. Use it for preparation instructions, verification results and errors the person must act on.
A surface that groups related content: a result, a team, an appointment. Cards are white and float on the paper; three variants set how loud they are.
Line, bar and donut charts plus a sparkline, drawn with thin marks, a quiet grid and one axis. Use a line for change over time, bars for magnitude across categories and a donut for parts of a whole.
Turns one option on or off, or picks any number from a list. For a setting that takes effect immediately, use a Switch.
An applied filter or a selected person that can be removed. ChipGroup animates chips as they are added and taken away. For a status that cannot be removed, use a Badge.
A single label that shows and hides one piece of content in place. Use it for detail most people do not need; use Accordion for a list of sections.
A searchable dropdown for long lists such as clinicians, lab tests or pharmacies. Combobox picks one item and MultiCombobox picks several.
Search-and-jump for the whole app: patients, pages and actions in one list, opened with ⌘K. One per app, mounted at the root.
A menu that opens where you right-click or long-press. Use it as a shortcut on rows, cards and records, never as the only route to an action.
Copies a value to the clipboard and confirms in place. Put it beside identifiers people paste elsewhere: MRNs, member IDs, claim numbers, links.

A table that sorts, hides columns, selects rows and paginates, with a toolbar slot and an empty state. Use it for any list of records people work through; it replaces the hand-written tables in the provider app.
A form field that opens a calendar. DatePicker chooses one day and DateRangePicker chooses a start and an end. To show the month grid on the page itself, use Calendar.
Label and value pairs in one, two or three columns. Use it for demographics, order details and claim fields: facts someone reads, not edits.
A window over the page for a task that needs the person's full attention: a question, a short form, a summary. Use a sheet when the page should stay in view.
What an area shows before it has content, or when a search finds nothing. It says what will be here and offers the action that fills it.
Field groups a label, a control, help text and an error message, and wires up the ids and aria attributes between them. Wrap every form control in one.
A drop zone and a list of the files added, with progress and errors per file. It works by click and keyboard as well as drag, and leaves the upload itself to you.
Clear glass panes, Frost and FrostDisc, for content that sits on the aurora surface or on a photograph. They are not for plain surfaces.

One highlight that moves between items instead of each item lighting up on its own. It is the system's signature movement, already built into menus, lists, tabs and the sidebar; use it directly when you build a new set of rows or links.
A preview shown when a link is hovered or focused: a clinician, a patient, a code. It is a shortcut, never the only way to reach the information.
A single-line text field in three sizes with room for an icon or a unit, plus Textarea for longer text and SearchInput for filtering lists.
A keyboard key, for shortcut hints in menus, tooltips, search fields and help panels.
A vertical list of rows with a leading slot, title, description and trailing value. Use it for inboxes, work queues and settings menus, where each row is one thing to open or do.
A list of actions that opens from a button. Use it for the secondary actions of a page, card or table row; use Select to choose a value.
A measured amount against a known range: capacity, adherence, a goal. Use Progress for work that is under way.
Four motion helpers: NumberTicker for summary figures, Reveal and RevealGroup for content that enters on scroll, and Parallax for decorative layers. All of them respect the reduced motion setting.
The system's signature form: a card with one corner cut away in a curve and its single action resting in the cut. Use it for the few cards on a page that lead somewhere.
A number with minus and plus buttons, for small counts such as refills, tablets or days supply. For free-form measurements use an Input with a unit.
One box per digit for one-time codes at sign-in and kiosk check-in. It accepts a pasted code and tells you when every digit is filled.
Moves through a long list one page at a time. DataTable has it built in, so reach for this only with lists and tables you assemble yourself.
A small frosted panel that opens from its trigger on click. Use it for a longer explanation or a quick edit that does not deserve a dialog.
A bar or a ring for work that is under way: a form being filled in, a file uploading. Use Meter for a measured amount and Segments for a few known steps.
Chooses exactly one of a few options that should all stay visible. For more than five options use a Select.
A region that scrolls inside a fixed height with a thin scrollbar that shows only while in use. Use it for long lists and text inside panels, sheets and cards.
A compact single choice between two to five views, such as Day, Week and Month. It is always controlled and always has one option selected.
Progress as a row of equal segments, one per step. Use it when the number of steps is small and known; use Progress for a percentage.
Chooses one option from a short, fixed list. For more than about ten options, or when people know what they are looking for, use a Combobox.
A hairline that divides content, horizontal or vertical. Try spacing first: a separator is for groups that white space alone does not tell apart.
A panel that slides in from an edge and keeps the page in context. Use it for detail views, filters and mobile navigation.
A shimmering placeholder with the shape of the content it stands in for. Use it while a page, card or list is loading; use Spinner for a short wait on an action.
Picks a number or a range by dragging along a track. Use it when the rough position matters more than the exact figure, such as a pain score.

A wrapper that animates its own height to follow its content. Use it around lists and panels that gain or lose content, so the layout resizes in one move instead of snapping. Data table uses it already.
Indeterminate progress for a short wait, such as a button or a line of status. Prefer Skeleton when content is loading and Progress when the amount is known.
Shows where someone is in a multi-step flow such as intake or booking. It displays progress only: the Back and Continue buttons are yours.
The app's small celebration for a finished flow: a check with a ring and a few brand-coloured particles. Use it once, at the end of something that took effort.
Turns a single setting on or off, effective immediately. Use it for preferences such as notifications, not for choices that are submitted with a form.
The plain table parts: header, body, rows and cells. Use it for static tables of a known size. For sorting, selection or pagination use Data table.
Switches between panels of related content without leaving the page. Three looks: underline for page sections, boxed for stages, segmented for views inside a card.
Free-text entries collected as tags: allergies, diagnosis codes, email recipients. When the options are known in advance, use a MultiCombobox instead.
Chooses a time of day from a list at a fixed step, for schedule blocks and reminders. For bookable appointment slots use the TimeSlots pattern.
Dated entries joined by a line. Use it for encounter history, order tracking and activity logs, where the order of events is the point.
A brief message that confirms what just happened, called with toast.success() and friends from anywhere. Errors the person must fix belong inline, next to their cause.
A set of on and off buttons for filters, days of the week or formatting. Pass multiple to allow several at once.
A small label that appears on hover or focus. Use it to name an icon button or add a hint; anything the person needs to read belongs on the page or in a popover.
The frame shared by the patient and provider apps: a collapsible sidebar and the content area beside it. Use it once, at the root of an app.
One appointment: date, time, who it is with, how it happens and its status. Use it in upcoming and past visit lists in both apps.
Message bubbles, a typing indicator and a composer. Use them for secure messaging between patients and the care team and for conversations with Pulse.
One lab result shown against its reference range, with the status in words. Use it wherever a patient or clinician reads results.
One medication: name, strength, directions in plain words, refills and status. Use it in medication lists in both apps.
The single header every screen uses: title, optional description, navigation above and actions at the end. It replaces the per-module headers in both apps.
The identity strip at the top of a patient chart: name, MRN, key facts and safety flags. Use it on every chart view in the provider app so the clinician always knows whose record is open.
One day of a clinician's schedule on an hour grid, with a line for the current time. Use one for a day view, or several side by side for a week or a multi-provider view.
One figure with its label and its change against a comparison period. Lay several out in a row for the summary strip at the top of a dashboard.
Available appointment times as a grid of choices. Pair it with Calendar in a booking flow, where the person picks a day and then a time.
One vital sign with its unit, when it was measured and its recent trend. Use it on the patient's home screen and in the chart summary.
